stimulus.text: From the Great Awakening through the period leading up to independence, Protestant evangelical ministers spoke of “liberty” and “virtue” delivering their congregants from “bondage and servitude.” The Boston Baptist minister John Allen's Oration Upon the Beauties of Liberty (1772), answering the Gaspee affair, was reprinted seven times in four cities. Evangelicals and republicans increasingly shared a language of opposition and resistance, likening British rule to the devil and urging colonists to resist corruption.

books.section: A. Protestant Evangelicalism and Enlightenment Philosophy

stem: What does the reprinting of John Allen's Oration Upon the Beauties of Liberty — seven times in four cities — most clearly show?

options.text: That the sermon was popular and widely read
That Allen was appointed to lead the Continental Congress
options.misconception: Allen was a Boston Baptist minister, not a member of Congress. Reprints show readers, not office.

options.text: That the Gaspee affair was forgotten soon after it happened
options.misconception: Seven reprints show the opposite — the sermon and the affair it answered stayed in circulation.

options.text: That the British government approved of Allen's message
options.misconception: The British prosecuted the Gaspee affair; a sermon attacking British rule would not win their approval.

rationales.A: Seven reprints in four cities means printers kept finding buyers — the sermon traveled far and was read widely. A text reprinted that often is a text in demand.
rationales.B: Allen held no office in Congress. Reprinting measures readers, not appointments.
rationales.C: Reprinting keeps a text alive. Seven printings show the Gaspee affair stayed in public memory.
rationales.D: The British were the sermon's target, not its patrons. Approval from London is the last thing it would earn.
rationales.general:
1. Count the printings. Seven times, in four cities — printers reprint what sells.
2. Ask what selling means. Readers in four cities wanted the sermon enough to pay for it.
3. Name the result. A popular sermon, widely read, carrying its argument far beyond one Boston pulpit.
Remember: reprints are votes with money — when a text is printed again and again, readers are choosing it.
